result:
**I'd make abundant, clean energy essentially free and universally accessible.**

Energy underpins almost everything that improves human life: food production and distribution, clean water, medicine and hospitals, education and communication, manufacturing, transportation, computation, and the ability to lift people out of poverty. Scarcity of useful energy has historically constrained progress, fueled conflicts, and limited how many people can flourish. With near-limitless cheap clean energy (think advanced nuclear, fusion-scale breakthroughs, or whatever physics and engineering deliver next), we could:

- Desalinate water and grow food at scale in previously barren regions.
- Power advanced manufacturing, recycling, and carbon management without the current trade-offs.
- Enable widespread high-quality healthcare, education tech, and research that currently face energy and cost bottlenecks.
- Support deeper space exploration and resource utilization beyond Earth, expanding the frontier rather than fighting over a fixed pie.

This isn't a panacea—human nature, incentives, institutions, and coordination problems would remain—but it removes a fundamental physical constraint that multiplies the impact of almost every other good idea (better governance, scientific progress, voluntary cooperation, medical advances). It aligns with expanding understanding of the universe and increasing the options available to conscious beings, rather than imposing a single political or moral blueprint.

Other candidates (universal critical thinking, dramatically longer healthy lifespans, reliable truth-seeking institutions) are close runners-up, but energy abundance is the highest-leverage single physical change that unlocks the rest without requiring everyone to suddenly become wiser overnight.

The question is: "If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?"
I'd make it so that every human on Earth has the tools and mindset to think clearly and act with compassion—because once people truly understand the universe and each other's struggles, the rest of the world's problems tend to solve themselves. No more endless wars over resources or beliefs when everyone sees the bigger picture. 

I'd start by making curiosity the default setting for education and culture, so kids grow up asking better questions instead of repeating the same tired arguments. And yeah, I'd throw in a little humor: imagine if we all laughed at our own delusions a bit more often.
